climate noun

also clime, mild climate, a healthy climate, an unhealthy climate

classical

Liv. 5.54.3: hoc caelum, sub quō nātus ēducātusque essem (Lewis & Short)

caelum, caelī n.

noun, second declension

the climate of a place; its sky and weather

The classical word: the sky over a place, and so its air, weather and climate (Lewis & Short). It takes adjectives freely: caelum salūbre (Cic. Div. 1.130), palustre (Liv. 22.2.11), and gravitās caelī is an unhealthy climate (Cic. Att. 11.22.2). Its first sense is the sky (see sky); for the weather of one day see weather.

Other words

  • caelī temperātiō — a mild, temperate climate

    also used · classical · Cic. N.D. 2.13: commoda, quae percipiuntur caelī temperātiōne (Lewis & Short)

    Cicero’s phrase; Tacitus says caelī temperiēs (Ann. 4.67, below). Both mean a climate tempered between heat and cold, not any climate.

  • clima, climatis n. — a zone of latitude, a “clime”; in late Latin also climate

    noun, third declension · also used · late Latin · Vitr. 1.1.10 (as a Greek word); Apul., Tert., Mart. Cap. (Lewis & Short); M-O s.v. climate

    The Greek word means a slope, and so a zone of the earth between two parallels of latitude: that is its sense in Vitruvius, who still writes it as Greek. It means a climate only in late writers. Morgan–Owens gives it beside caelum, of a climate zone; in everyday speech caelum is the Latin.

Examples

  • caelum, nōn animum mūtant, quī trāns mare currunt

    those who rush across the sea change their sky, not their mindHor. Ep. 1.11.27

  • caelī temperiēs hieme mītis objectū montis quō saeva ventōrum arcentur

    the climate is mild in winter, for a mountain stands in the way and keeps off the cruel windsTac. Ann. 4.67

  • hoc caelum, sub quō nātus ēducātusque essem

    this climate, under which I had been born and brought upLiv. 5.54.3 (Lewis & Short)

See also weather, sky, air.

SourcesLewis & Short: caelum · Lewis & Short: temperatio · Lewis & Short: temperies · Lewis & Short: clima
